XCSSET v40 outbound retrieval to rotating C2 module/binary paths (/s/, /d/) AICommand & Control Low
Hunts macOS developer-host outbound traffic to the XCSSET v40 rotating C2 endpoints that serve Base64+AES-encrypted modules (/s/<module>) and binaries (/d/<binary>). Because domains rotate, this pivots on the distinctive short-first-segment path plus a rotated token, excluding browser processes. Rationale: Uses the article's C2 path matrix — GET /s/<rotated_module_name> and GET /d/<rotated_binary_name> serving Base64+AES payloads. Domains rotate so path+token is the durable pivot; excluding browsers and requiring a >=6-char token reduces (but does not eliminate) noise, hence Low confidence. Cross-checked against: • https://cybersecuritynews.com/xcsset-v40-abuses-chrome-devtools/ • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/new-xcsset-variant-targets-macos-devs-via-compromised-xcode-projects/
ATT&CKT1105 T1041 T1071.001
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: high — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • CDNs and object stores that use /s/ or /d/ short path prefixes with hashed tokens (e.g. some static asset or shortlink services)
  • Package registries or download mirrors serving artifacts under /d/
  • Legitimate CLI tools (curl/python) fetching signed URLs with random tokens
  • API SDKs using single-letter path segments
Suppression filter
| where not(RemoteUrl has_any ("amazonaws.com","cloudfront.net","githubusercontent.com","fastly.net","akamai"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: resolve the destination host, check age/reputation and whether it also serves POST /u (exfil) or /l (logging); confirm the initiating process is a shell/curl/osascript rather than a known updater. 2) Contain: block the host at the proxy/firewall, isolate the endpoint, and capture the initiating process tree. 3) Hunt: correlate with chrome_remote execution, Chrome --remote-debugging-port launches, and .pbxproj modifications on the same host to confirm a full XCSSET v40 chain, then sweep peers for the same destination.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where isnotempty(RemoteUrl)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("Google Chrome","Google Chrome Helper","Safari","firefox","Microsoft Edge","com.apple.WebKit.Networking","nsurlsessiond")
| where RemoteUrl matches regex @"(?i)/(s|d)/[A-Za-z0-9_+/=\-]{6,}"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where Url matches regex @"(?i)/(s|d)/[A-Za-z0-9_+/=\-]{6,}"
| project TimeGenerated, SrcHostname, SrcIpAddr, SrcUsername, Url, HttpMethod, DstIpAddr, DstHostname
| order by TimeGenerated desc
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2
| ImageFileName=/\/(curl|osascript|bash|sh|zsh|python3?)$/i
| CommandLine=/https?:\/\/[^ ]+\/(s|d)\/[A-Za-z0-9_+\/=\-]{6,}/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ImageFileName, CommandLine], function=count())
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic where All_Traffic.url IN ("*/s/*","*/d/*") All_Traffic.app!="Google Chrome" All_Traffic.app!="Safari" by All_Traffic.src All_Traffic.dest All_Traffic.url All_Traffic.app | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)` | regex url="/(s|d)/[A-Za-z0-9_+/=\-]{6,}" | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime) | sort - lastTime
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic where All_Traffic.url IN ("*/s/*","*/d/*") All_Traffic.app!="Google Chrome" All_Traffic.app!="Safari" by All_Traffic.src All_Traffic.dest All_Traffic.url All_Traffic.app | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)` | regex url="/(s|d)/[A-Za-z0-9_+/=\-]{6,}" | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime) | sort - lastTime
Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

AWS Amplify UI Builder CreateComponent/UpdateComponent — CVE-2025-4318 malicious schema injection AIInstallation Medium
Hunts AmplifyUIBuilder CreateComponent/UpdateComponent/ExportComponent CloudTrail events, the exact API path an authenticated principal uses to import a component schema whose property bindings carry arbitrary JavaScript (CVE-2025-4318). The injected expression re-executes during every codegen/render/build, so the create/update call is the persistence-planting event to surface and attribute to a principal + source IP. Rationale: Uses the concrete eventSource amplifyuibuilder.amazonaws.com and the CreateComponent/UpdateComponent/ExportComponent API names named in the advisory (and confirmed in the AmplifyUIBuilder API reference) — the exact and only path a malicious component schema is imported through. Cross-checked against: • https://aws.amazon.com/security/security-bulletins/AWS-2025-010/ • https://docs.aws.amazon.com/amplifyuibuilder/latest/APIReference/API_CreateComponent.html • https://advisories.gitlab.com/npm/@aws-amplify/codegen-ui-react/CVE-2025-4318/
ATT&CKT1059.007 T1195.002
Data sourcesChange.All_Changes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate developers building/editing UI Builder components in Amplify Studio during normal front-end development
  • Amplify Studio auto-generating components from a DataStore/GraphQL schema import
  • CI service role programmatically syncing components as part of an IaC/export workflow
  • QA or design teams iterating on forms/views/themes
  • First-time Amplify Studio onboarding generating starter components in bulk
Suppression filter
| where userIdentity.type != "AssumedRole" or requestParameters.name has_any ("eval","constructor","process","require","${")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the userIdentity.arn, sourceIPAddress and componentName; confirm the principal is an expected Amplify developer and the IP/geo matches normal dev activity. Retrieve the component schema (GetComponent) and inspect bindingProperties/collectionProperties for expression-like or JS payloads (e.g. constructor, process, require, backtick/${} expressions). 2) Contain: if the schema contains code, delete/roll back the component, rotate the principal's credentials, and freeze codegen builds that pull it (amplify pull / ampx) until packages are on @aws-amplify/codegen-ui(-react) >= 2.20.4. 3) Hunt: enumerate all CreateComponent/UpdateComponent by that principal, check build-host/CI process telemetry for anomalous node child processes at codegen time, and inventory repos for vulnerable codegen-ui versions <=2.20.2.

AWS Amplify UI Builder create-component CLI invocation on endpoint/CI host (CVE-2025-4318) AIExploitation Medium
Hunts process executions of the AWS CLI 'amplifyuibuilder create-component/update-component/export-component' commands on developer workstations and CI/build runners — the client-side action that imports a component schema and (for vulnerable <=2.20.2 codegen-ui) triggers arbitrary JavaScript during local codegen/build. Complements the CloudTrail UC by catching the on-host command line and its parent process. Rationale: Anchors on the exact 'create-component' command named in the advisory (plus the update/export variants that share the vulnerable binding path) scoped by the 'amplifyuibuilder' service token, so it fires only on Amplify UI Builder schema imports rather than generic AWS CLI usage. Cross-checked against: • https://aws.amazon.com/security/security-bulletins/AWS-2025-010/ • https://docs.aws.amazon.com/amplifyuibuilder/latest/APIReference/API_CreateComponent.html
ATT&CKT1059.007 T1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Front-end developers legitimately importing/exporting components via aws amplifyuibuilder in local dev
  • CI/CD pipeline steps that scriptaws amplifyuibuilder export-component for codegen
  • Infrastructure-as-code sync jobs recreating components from JSON definitions
  • Amplify migration/backup scripts bulk-exporting components
  • Automated tests that provision throwaway components
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("jenkins-agent.exe","runner.worker.exe","buildkitd.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: capture the full ProcessCommandLine and any --cli-input-json / --component-to-create payload path; open the referenced schema and inspect property bindings for JS (eval, constructor, require, ${}, backticks). Confirm whether the host's node_modules ships @aws-amplify/codegen-ui(-react) <=2.20.2. 2) Contain: on a confirmed malicious schema, isolate the build host/CI runner, kill child node/codegen processes, and block the build from publishing artifacts; upgrade codegen-ui to >=2.20.4 before re-running. 3) Hunt: correlate to the CloudTrail CreateComponent/UpdateComponent event by the same identity/time, review that principal's other Amplify actions, and sweep all build hosts for the vulnerable package version.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ProcessCommandLine has "amplifyuibuilder"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("create-component","update-component","export-component")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where CommandLine has "amplifyuibuilder"
| where CommandLine has_any ("create-component","update-component","export-component")
| where not(SubjectUserName endswith "$")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Installation of compromised @joyfill/components or @joyfill/layouts 2773 beta packages AIDelivery High
Hunts for npm/yarn/pnpm invocations that install the hijacked @joyfill/components or @joyfill/layouts prerelease versions carrying the 2773 marker. Rationale: Anchors on the exact compromised package names plus the '2773' campaign version marker from the article's IOC table; the beta tags are never installed transitively so an explicit reference is near-certain compromise. Node.js host callout to Joyfill DEV#POPPER RAT C2 infrastructure AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts outbound connections to the four confirmed Joyfill RAT command-and-control IPs (Socket.IO C2 and /$/boot second-stage host). Because the payload runs in-process under Node.js, any host reaching these IPs after importing the package indicates live RAT activity. Rationale: Uses the four verified C2 IPs from the article's IOC block (166.88.134.62 on 443/80, 23.27.13.43 serving /$/boot, 198.105.127.210, 23.27.202.27); direct IP hits are unambiguous. Projecting InitiatingProcessFileName surfaces the offending node.exe without hard-coding a PID. Cross-checked against: • https://socket.dev/blog/joyfill-npm-beta-releases-compromised • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/two-compromised-joyfill-npm-packages.html
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1041
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Shared/bulletproof hosting IP later reassigned to a benign service
  • Threat-intel platform actively probing the C2 IP
  • Security proxy/sandbox detonation reaching the IP during analysis
  • Reverse-DNS or connectivity checks by a monitoring tool
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the initiating process (expect node.exe) and confirm the host has a compromised @joyfill version in node_modules. 2) Contain: block the four C2 IPs at egress, isolate the host, and kill the node process; treat the workstation as compromised and rotate developer credentials. 3) Hunt: search DeviceNetworkEvents for the C2 request paths /$/boot, /u/e, /u/f, /0x/js, /verify-human/, /snv and for blockchain-resolver traffic to api.trongrid.io and bsc-dataseed.binance.org from the same host.

| where RemoteIP in ("166.88.134.62","23.27.13.43","198.105.127.210","23.27.202.27")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl
| order by Timestamp desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DstIpAddr in ("166.88.134.62","23.27.13.43","198.105.127.210","23.27.202.27")
| project TimeGenerated, SrcHostname, SrcIpAddr, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber, NetworkApplicationProtocol, Url, DvcHostname
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Node.js spawning a shell or detached node -e child (Joyfill RAT execution) AIExploitation Medium
Hunts for node.exe spawning cmd/PowerShell/script hosts or a detached 'node -e' child, matching the RAT's ss_eval arbitrary-execution verb and the article's detached 'node -e' stage that fetches /$/boot. Pairs a node parent with a suspicious child to turn generic exec into an article-specific signal. Rationale: Grounded in the article's 'spawns a detached node -e child' behaviour and the RAT's ss_eval arbitrary-execution verb; the node.exe→shell / node.exe→node -e parent-child pairing narrows generic interpreter execution to the implant's shape. Cross-checked against: • https://socket.dev/blog/joyfill-npm-beta-releases-compromised
ATT&CKT1059.007 T1059
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Build scripts / npm run hooks legitimately invoking node -e for scripting
  • Electron/dev tooling shelling out to cmd.exe for platform tasks
  • Test runners spawning child_process shells
  • CI pipelines using node to orchestrate PowerShell steps
  • Local dev servers spawning cross-platform helpers
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("node_modules\\.bin","npm run","jest","webpack","vite","eslint"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: inspect the child command line — benign build hooks reference project paths; RAT activity references reconnaissance, /$/boot fetches, or credential paths. 2) Contain: if the parent node process traces to a compromised @joyfill import, isolate the host and kill the process tree. 3) Hunt: correlate with DeviceNetworkEvents to the four C2 IPs and check DeviceFileEvents for the Python infostealer staging and dev-tool module tampering on the same host.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "node.exe"
| where (FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe"))
     or (FileName =~ "node.exe" and ProcessCommandLine has " -e ")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "\\node.exe"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\\cmd.exe" or NewProcessName endswith "\\powershell.exe" or NewProcessName endswith "\\pwsh.exe" or NewProcessName endswith "\\wscript.exe" or NewProcessName endswith "\\cscript.exe" or (NewProcessName endswith "\\node.exe" and CommandLine has " -e ")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Joyfill RAT persistence injection into developer tool modules (VS Code / Discord / GitHub Desktop / npm) AIInstallation High
Hunts for node.exe modifying the specific developer-tool JavaScript files the RAT self-reloads through: the @vscode/deviceid module, the Discord desktop core module, GitHub Desktop main.js, and the global npm CLI. Legitimate updates to these apps are not driven by node.exe, making a node-initiated write to them high-fidelity persistence evidence. Rationale: Directly encodes the article's named persistence targets (@vscode/deviceid, Discord desktop core, GitHub Desktop main.js, global npm CLI) and requires node.exe as the writer, which legitimate app self-updates never are. Cross-checked against: • https://socket.dev/blog/joyfill-npm-beta-releases-compromised • https://cybersecuritynews.com/hijacked-joyfill-npm-packages-worm-like-rat/
ATT&CKT1554 T1195.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer running a local npm/VS Code extension build that regenerates deviceid modules
  • Electron app rebuild pipeline rewriting Discord/GitHub Desktop bundles from source
  • Custom internal tooling patching npm CLI via node scripts
  • Antivirus quarantine restore rewriting a .js file
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("npm run build","electron-rebuild","webpack"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: diff the modified JS file against a pristine copy of the app/module; the RAT inserts a self-reloading block referencing require/module bootstrap. 2) Contain: isolate the host, restore the affected modules from clean installers, and remove the compromised @joyfill package; rotate developer credentials. 3) Hunt: search for the Python infostealer archive staging, the C2 IP callouts, and the same node-initiated writes across other developer endpoints (worm-like propagation).

| where FileName endswith ".js"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FolderPath, FileName, ActionType, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent

| where TargetFileName endswith ".js"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, TargetFileSHA256
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Known-malicious Joyfill package bundle hash observed on disk AIInstallation Medium
Alerts on the presence of any of the three confirmed SHA256 hashes of the obfuscated Joyfill RAT distribution bundles on an endpoint. This is an exact-match indicator that removes ambiguity even when package version strings or paths are altered. Rationale: Uses the three exact SHA256 hashes published in the article's IOC block for the obfuscated malicious bundles; hash matches are unambiguous. Falcon FileWritten carries no hash field so falcon_logscale_query is intentionally empty. Cross-checked against: • https://socket.dev/blog/joyfill-npm-beta-releases-compromised
ATT&CKT1027 T1195.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Malware analyst storing the sample in a controlled repo
  • Detection-engineering IOC validation copying the file for testing
  • Backup/EDR quarantine artifact retaining a copy of the bundle
Suppression filter
| where not (FolderPath has_any ("\\Quarantine\\","\\malware-samples\\","\\sandbox\\"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the file path is inside a real node_modules/@joyfill tree versus an analyst sandbox. 2) Contain: quarantine the file, isolate the host, and remove the compromised package version; rotate developer credentials on the host. 3) Hunt: sweep the estate for the same three hashes and pivot to the C2 IP callouts and dev-tool persistence writes on any host that matches.

| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FolderPath, FileName, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc

Compromised @joyfill package artifacts written under node_modules or lock files AIInstallation Medium
Hunts for the filesystem footprint of the hijacked packages landing on disk: the specific dist bundle filenames under node_modules/@joyfill/{components,layouts}, plus lock-file writes by a package manager that would pin the compromised release. Complements the process-based install detection with a filesystem-side pivot that survives shell/CI variations. Rationale: Anchors on the exact dist bundle filenames the article says carry the payload (index.js/index.esm.js/joyfill.min.js for components; index.cjs.js/index.es.js for layouts) under node_modules/@joyfill, giving a filesystem pivot independent of the install command line. Cross-checked against: • https://socket.dev/blog/joyfill-npm-beta-releases-compromised
ATT&CKT1195.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate install of a clean @joyfill version writing the same dist filenames (join to hash/version to confirm)
  • Routine package-lock.json regeneration during any npm install
  • Monorepo dependency hoisting rewriting node_modules trees
  • yarn/pnpm cache restore on CI recreating node_modules
Suppression filter
| where not (FolderPath has "\\.cache\\" or FolderPath has "\\Yarn\\Cache\\")
Response runbook
1) Triage: read the package.json version alongside the dist write and compare against 4.0.0-rc24-2773-beta.4/5/6 or 0.1.2-2773.beta.0/1/2, or hash the dist file against the three known-bad SHA256s. 2) Contain: if the version/hash matches, remove the package, pin to a pre-2026-07-28 release, and isolate the host. 3) Hunt: pivot to node.exe C2 callouts and to persistence writes in @vscode/deviceid, Discord, GitHub Desktop, and the npm CLI.

   or (FileName in~ ("package-lock.json","yarn.lock","pnpm-lock.yaml") and InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("npm.exe","node.exe","yarn.exe","pnpm.exe"))
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FolderPath, FileName, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine

| TargetFileName=/(index\.js|index\.esm\.js|joyfill\.min\.js|index\.cjs\.js|index\.es\.js|package\.json)$/i

| tstats summariesonly=false count from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where (Filesystem.file_path=*node_modules\\@joyfill\\components* OR Filesystem.file_path=*node_modules\\@joyfill\\layouts*) (Filesystem.file_name IN (index.js,index.esm.js,joyfill.min.js,index.cjs.js,index.es.js,package.json)) by Filesystem.dest Filesystem.file_path Filesystem.file_name Filesystem.file_hash | `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
Network connections to article IPs / domains Command & Control High
Outbound traffic to attacker infrastructure named in the article.
ATT&CKT1071
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic Web Network_Resolution.DNS DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where RemoteIP in ("166.88.134.62", "23.27.13.43", "198.105.127.210", "23.27.202.27") or RemoteUrl has_any ("api.trongrid.io", "fullnode.mainnet.aptoslabs.com", "bsc-dataseed.binance.org", "bsc-rpc.publicnode.com", "ip-api.com")

let BadIPs     = dynamic(["166.88.134.62", "23.27.13.43", "198.105.127.210", "23.27.202.27"]);
let BadDomains = dynamic(["api.trongrid.io", "fullnode.mainnet.aptoslabs.com", "bsc-dataseed.binance.org", "bsc-rpc.publicnode.com", "ip-api.com"]);
ImNetworkSession

Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs Actions on Objectives High
Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies SQLite from Chrome/Edge/Firefox.
ATT&CKT1539 T1555.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where FolderPath has_any (@"\Google\Chrome\User Data\", @"\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\", @"\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\")
| where FileName in~ ("Login Data","Cookies","logins.json","cookies.sqlite")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FolderPath, FileName, ActionType

// ASIM ImFileEvent — covers MDE, Sysmon, AuditD, Defender for Cloud, etc.
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where TargetFilePath has_any (@"\Google\Chrome\User Data\",
                                  @"\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\",
                                  @"\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\")
| where TargetFileName in~ ("Login Data","Cookies","logins.json","cookies.sqlite")
| where ActingProcessName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName,
          TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, EventType

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command Exploitation High
Encoded or obfuscated PowerShell — common across loaders, recon, and post-exploitation.
ATT&CKT1059.001 T1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)(-enc|encodedcommand|frombase64string|-nop|-w\s+hidden|invoke-expression|iex\s*\(|downloadstring|net\.webclient)"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\pwsh.exe"
| where CommandLine matches regex @"(?i)(-enc|encodedcommand|frombase64string|-nop|-w\s+hidden|invoke-expression|iex\s*\(|downloadstring|net\.webclient)"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName,
          CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Obfuscated / Encoded PowerShell Execution
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d08
status: experimental
description: |
    PowerShell launched with -EncodedCommand, base64 strings, hidden
    window, no-profile, bypass policy, IEX / Invoke-Expression / Net
    .WebClient.DownloadString — combinations indicating evasion.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/001/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1027/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1059.001
    - attack.t1027
    - attack.execution
    - attack.defense-evasion
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_image:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
    selection_args:
        CommandLine|contains:
            - '-enc '
            - 'EncodedCommand'
            - 'FromBase64String'
            - 'Invoke-Expression'
            - 'IEX('
            - 'DownloadString'
            - 'Net.WebClient'
            - '-w hidden'
            - '-WindowStyle Hidden'
            - '-nop'
            - '-NoProfile'
            - '-ep bypass'
            - '-ExecutionPolicy Bypass'
    condition: selection_image and selection_args
falsepositives:
    - DevOps tooling that legitimately uses encoded command for
      cross-shell escaping
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*-enc *" OR Processes.process="*EncodedCommand*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64String*" OR Processes.process="*-nop*"
        OR Processes.process="*-w hidden*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*IEX(*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*Net.WebClient*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*-enc *" OR Processes.process="*EncodedCommand*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64String*" OR Processes.process="*-nop*"
        OR Processes.process="*-w hidden*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*IEX(*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*Net.WebClient*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children Exploitation Medium
Supply-chain trojan signal: legitimate signed binary spawning script interpreters or exotic LOLBins.
ATT&CKT1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","cmd.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
// Replace `"setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe"` with the vendor binaries observed in the
// article (matching shape with the Defender query).
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
| where NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\rundll32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\regsvr32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wmic.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\bitsadmin.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Trusted Vendor Binary Launching Unusual Children
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d09
status: experimental
description: |
    A signed vendor binary (in the article's named-vendors list)
    spawning script-host or LOLBin children. Strongest signal when
    paired with a recent CVE / supply-chain advisory naming the same
    vendor.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1195/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1195
    - attack.initial-access
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\cmd.exe'
            - '\rundll32.exe'
            - '\regsvr32.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
            - '\wscript.exe'
            - '\cscript.exe'
            - '\wmic.exe'
            - '\bitsadmin.exe'
    selection_parent_vendor:
        ParentImage|contains:
            - '\Program Files\'
            - '\Program Files (x86)\'

      the parent path to specific vendor binaries observed in the
      article before alerting.
level: medium

    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("26351aed0397158d3a3b8cc8fd3047d4c015d264c9895f10f20f1521b974ed18", "36ff00b45e67baa7e3674b0c80f48e88737264c61e5c6b3b091200972de8157c", "cb46f12d70824ea24ed1f8bcf45bf3f86680e02a9089aafc03b27f691be57be3") or SHA1 in~ ("26351aed0397158d3a3b8cc8fd3047d4c015d264c9895f10f20f1521b974ed18", "36ff00b45e67baa7e3674b0c80f48e88737264c61e5c6b3b091200972de8157c", "cb46f12d70824ea24ed1f8bcf45bf3f86680e02a9089aafc03b27f691be57be3") or MD5 in~ ("26351aed0397158d3a3b8cc8fd3047d4c015d264c9895f10f20f1521b974ed18", "36ff00b45e67baa7e3674b0c80f48e88737264c61e5c6b3b091200972de8157c", "cb46f12d70824ea24ed1f8bcf45bf3f86680e02a9089aafc03b27f691be57be3")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("26351aed0397158d3a3b8cc8fd3047d4c015d264c9895f10f20f1521b974ed18", "36ff00b45e67baa7e3674b0c80f48e88737264c61e5c6b3b091200972de8157c", "cb46f12d70824ea24ed1f8bcf45bf3f86680e02a9089aafc03b27f691be57be3") or SHA1 in~ ("26351aed0397158d3a3b8cc8fd3047d4c015d264c9895f10f20f1521b974ed18", "36ff00b45e67baa7e3674b0c80f48e88737264c61e5c6b3b091200972de8157c", "cb46f12d70824ea24ed1f8bcf45bf3f86680e02a9089aafc03b27f691be57be3") or MD5 in~ ("26351aed0397158d3a3b8cc8fd3047d4c015d264c9895f10f20f1521b974ed18", "36ff00b45e67baa7e3674b0c80f48e88737264c61e5c6b3b091200972de8157c", "cb46f12d70824ea24ed1f8bcf45bf3f86680e02a9089aafc03b27f691be57be3")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["26351aed0397158d3a3b8cc8fd3047d4c015d264c9895f10f20f1521b974ed18", "36ff00b45e67baa7e3674b0c80f48e88737264c61e5c6b3b091200972de8157c", "cb46f12d70824ea24ed1f8bcf45bf3f86680e02a9089aafc03b27f691be57be3"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] Ruby/Puma Rails web process spawns a shell (post-file-read RCE via forged secret_key_base cookie) · [LLM] Internet-facing hosts running activestorage vulnerable to CVE-2026-66066
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Rails web process reads /proc/self/environ or app secrets (Active Storage libvips file-read) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
Rails web process reads /proc/self/environ or app secrets (Active Storage libvips file-read) AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts the core arbitrary-file-read primitive of CVE-2026-66066: a crafted upload drives an unfuzzed libvips loader inside the Ruby/Puma process to read the process environment and Rails secrets (secret_key_base, master.key, credentials.yml.enc). Because libvips is linked into the app process, the read shows up as the web-app binary opening files it never touches at runtime. Rationale: Anchored on the exact read targets the GHSA names as the payoff (secret_key_base in the process environment, master.key, credentials.yml.enc) and scoped to the Ruby web-app process as the actor — that pairing is the file-read primitive itself, not a generic file-access rule. Confirmed via the advisory plus Ethiack and Flatt write-ups that the impact is disclosure of the process environment. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-xr9x-r78c-5hrm • https://ethiack.com/info-hub/research/kindarails2shell-rails-rce-cve • https://blog.flatt.tech/entry/kindarails2shell_rails • https://www.libvips.org/2022/05/28/What's-new-in-8.13.html
ATT&CKT1552.001 T1190
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Rails app legitimately reading config/master.key and config/credentials.yml.enc at boot (normal startup — not /proc/self/environ)
  • Backup or DLP agents reading /etc/passwd during scheduled scans
  • APM/observability agents (e.g. Datadog, New Relic) reading /proc/<pid>/environ for metadata enrichment
  • Config-management runs (Ansible/Chef) reading /etc/passwd or .env files
  • Container init scripts sourcing .env files at container start
Suppression filter
| where not (TargetFilePath has_any ("/config/master.key","/config/credentials.yml.enc") and ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("rails server","puma","bootsnap"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the actor is the web-app process (ruby/puma) and the read occurred mid-request (not at process start) — correlate the read timestamp against Active Storage variant/representation requests in the web/access log. 2) Contain: if /proc/self/environ or /etc/passwd was read by the app process, treat secret_key_base and every env-resident credential as exposed — rotate secret_key_base, master.key, DB creds and S3/GCS/Azure Active Storage keys immediately (invalidates sessions). 3) Hunt: check for follow-on ruby-spawned shells and outbound connections from the host, and search web logs for the uploads that preceded the read (/rails/active_storage/representations/ and /rails/active_storage/direct_uploads).
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventType == "FileAccessed"
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("ruby","puma","passenger","rails")
| where TargetFilePath has_any ("/proc/self/environ","/environ","/etc/passwd","/config/master.key","/config/credentials.yml.enc","/.env")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessId, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFilePath, ActorUsername
| order by TimeGenerated desc
#event_simpleName=FileOpenInfo ContextImageFileName=/(ruby|puma|passenger|rails)/i
| TargetFileName=/(\/proc\/self\/environ|\/proc\/\d+\/environ|\/etc\/passwd|\/config\/master\.key|\/config\/credentials\.yml\.enc|\/\.env)$/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName, TargetFileName], function=count())

Ruby/Puma Rails web process spawns a shell (post-file-read RCE via forged secret_key_base cookie) AIExploitation Medium
Detects the RCE stage of CVE-2026-66066: after leaking secret_key_base, the attacker forges a signed/encrypted Rails cookie carrying a deserialization payload, yielding code execution inside the app process. Surfaces the anomalous child — an interactive shell or download tool spawned by the Ruby/Puma web worker. Rationale: The advisory states the file-read escalates to RCE via secrets in the process environment; the observable outcome is the Rails worker (ruby/puma/passenger) spawning a shell or fetch tool — a parent→child pair that is abnormal for a web app running the in-process :vips processor. Parents and children are all concrete binary names, no placeholders. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-xr9x-r78c-5hrm • https://blog.flatt.tech/entry/kindarails2shell_rails
ATT&CKT1059.004 T1190 T1505.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Rails apps that legitimately shell out via system()/backticks (e.g. running git, imagemagick/mini_magick, ffmpeg, or a rake task)
  • Deploy/boot scripts where puma is launched by a shell wrapper and re-execs sh
  • Health-check or cron jobs invoking curl/wget from within the app container
  • Background job workers (Sidekiq/Resque under ruby) shelling out to CLI tools by design
  • Container entrypoints where bundle exec spawns sh for pre-boot hooks
Suppression filter
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("/dev/tcp","-i ","sh -c","bash -c","-c 'curl","-c \"curl","base64 -d") or ProcessCommandLine !has_any ("git","convert","mogrify","ffmpeg","rake")
Response runbook
1) Triage: inspect ProcessCommandLine of the child — reverse-shell markers (/dev/tcp, -i, bash -c with piped curl) or interactive shells with no args are high-confidence; benign shell-outs name a specific tool/arg. Correlate against UC1 file-read hits on the same host. 2) Contain: isolate the host/pod, kill the offending Ruby worker, and rotate secret_key_base + all env-resident credentials (the RCE path depends on the leaked signing key). 3) Hunt: pull the preceding web requests to /rails/active_storage/representations/ and /rails/active_storage/direct_uploads, review outbound connections from the host, and check for persistence (cron, authorized_keys, new services).
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("ruby","ruby3.2","ruby3.3","puma","passenger","bundle","rails")
| where FileName in~ ("sh","bash","dash","zsh","nc","ncat","curl","wget","python","python3","perl")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, ProcessId
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("ruby","puma","passenger","bundle","rails")
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("/sh","/bash","/dash","/zsh","/nc","/ncat","/curl","/wget","/python","/perl")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Internet-facing hosts running activestorage vulnerable to CVE-2026-66066 AIExploitation High
Exposure hunt for the attack surface: hosts with an activestorage version affected by CVE-2026-66066 (< 7.2.3.2, 8.0.x < 8.0.5.1, 8.1.x < 8.1.3.1), prioritising internet-facing systems and those still on libvips < 8.13 which cannot block unfuzzed loaders. Drives patch/mitigation before the 2026-08-28 full disclosure. Rationale: Uses the exact CVE id and the vendor-published affected-version boundaries from the advisory; joining internet-facing status turns a raw inventory list into a ranked remediation queue for the specific gem in this CVE. No version-string math needed — the TVM CveId already encodes the affected ranges. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-xr9x-r78c-5hrm
ATT&CKT1190
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Hosts already patched to 7.2.3.2 / 8.0.5.1 / 8.1.3.1 but TVM inventory not yet refreshed (stale)
  • Apps that carry ruby-vips only for image analysis and never generate variants (lower real risk despite matching)
  • Hosts where libvips >= 8.13 is present and VIPS_BLOCK_UNTRUSTED / Vips.block_untrusted(true) is already set (mitigated without gem upgrade)
  • Non-production/staging boxes flagged as internet-facing by network heuristics but actually firewalled
Response runbook
1) Triage: for each hit confirm variant_processor is :vips (default since load_defaults 7.0) and whether the app accepts uploads from untrusted users — those two conditions gate real exploitability. 2) Contain: upgrade activestorage to the fixed release and ensure libvips >= 8.13; where an immediate upgrade isn't possible, set VIPS_BLOCK_UNTRUSTED=1 (or Vips.block_untrusted(true)) as an interim block, prioritising internet-facing hosts. 3) Hunt: on any host that was exposed before patching, assume secret exposure — rotate secret_key_base, master.key, DB and Active Storage service credentials, and run UC1/UC2 retrospectively over the exposure window.

| join kind=leftouter (DeviceInfo | summarize arg_max(Timestamp, IsInternetFacing, OSPlatform) by DeviceId) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, DeviceId, SoftwareVendor, SoftwareName, SoftwareVersion, RecommendedSecurityUpdate, IsInternetFacing, OSPlatform
| order by IsInternetFacing desc, DeviceName asc

| project DeviceName, DeviceId, SoftwareName, SoftwareVersion, RecommendedSecurityUpdate, IsInternetFacing, OSPlatform

| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId,

| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Successful Entra ID device-code authentication (ARToken/EvilTokens PhaaS MFA bypass) · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender

Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Zoho Assist Unattended Agent deployment (Warlock / Storm-2603 ransomware) · File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Trojanized MeshAgent running outside its install path (Sinobi ransomware C2) · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains

Successful Entra ID device-code authentication (ARToken/EvilTokens PhaaS MFA bypass) AIDelivery Medium
Hunts successful OAuth device-code grant sign-ins in Entra ID, the flow abused by the ARToken/EvilTokens phishing-as-a-service platform to bypass MFA and mint persistent refresh tokens. Device-code auth is rare/unused in most tenants, so any success warrants review for account takeover. Rationale: Grounds on the ARToken/EvilTokens device-code phishing pattern named in the corroborated Talos IR Q2 2026 report; device-code auth success is inherently rare and high-signal for token-theft AiTM. Cross-checked https://blog.talosintelligence.com/ir-trends-q2-2026/. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.talosintelligence.com/ir-trends-q2-2026/
ATT&CKT1621 T1528 T1566.002
Data sourcesAuthentication
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate device-code sign-in from IoT/kiosk/CLI tooling (Azure CLI 'az login --use-device-code')
  • Conference-room / smart-TV Teams device provisioning
  • Developers using device-code flow for headless service auth
  • PowerShell modules (Microsoft.Graph, Az) prompting device-code login on servers
Suppression filter
| where ClientAppUsed !in ("Mobile Apps and Desktop clients") or Application !has_any ("Microsoft Azure CLI","Microsoft Azure PowerShell","Microsoft Graph Command Line Tools")
Response runbook
1) Triage: For each hit, confirm whether the user legitimately performs device-code logins; check the IP/geo/ASN and UserAgent against the user's baseline and look for impossible travel. 2) Contain: If unrecognized, revoke sessions/refresh tokens (Revoke-MgUserSignInSession), force password reset, and re-register MFA; block the source IP. 3) Hunt: Pivot on the AccountUpn for subsequent non-interactive token use, new inbox rules, OAuth app consents, and mailbox/SharePoint access from the same IP.
AADSignInEventsBeta
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where AuthenticationProcessingDetails has "Device Code"
| where ErrorCode == 0            // successful device-code grant
| project Timestamp, AccountUpn, Application, ApplicationId, IPAddress, Country, City, UserAgent, ClientAppUsed
| order by Timestamp desc
SigninLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where AuthenticationProcessingDetails has "Device Code"
| where ResultType == 0           // successful device-code grant
| project TimeGenerated, UserPrincipalName, AppDisplayName, AppId, IPAddress, Location, UserAgent, ClientAppUsed
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Trojanized MeshAgent running outside its install path (Sinobi ransomware C2) AICommand & Control High
Hunts MeshAgent / MeshCentral processes executing from non-standard locations, the trojanized SYSTEM-level auto-start C2 used by Sinobi ransomware operators. Legitimate MeshCentral installs live under a fixed program path; execution elsewhere indicates an attacker-deployed agent. Rationale: Uses the corroborated report detail that Sinobi deployed a trojanized MeshAgent as SYSTEM auto-start C2; anchoring on the MeshAgent binary/product plus a path-exclusion turns a legit tool into a high-fidelity attacker signal. Cross-checked Talos IR Q2 2026 and detection.fyi renamed-MeshAgent Sigma. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.talosintelligence.com/ir-trends-q2-2026/ • https://detection.fyi/sigmahq/sigma/macos/process_creation/proc_creation_macos_remote_access_tools_renamed_meshagent_execution/
ATT&CKT1219 T1543.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Sanctioned MeshCentral deployment installed to a custom directory by IT
  • Portable MeshAgent run from a technician's USB during legitimate support
  • Security-team red-team or RMM evaluation testing
  • MSP-managed endpoints where MeshCentral is the approved RMM
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !in~ ("approved-rmm-svc") and SHA256 !in ("<known-good-meshagent-sha256-from-your-approved-build>")
Response runbook
1) Triage: Verify whether MeshCentral is an approved RMM for this host/business unit; inspect the file path, SHA256 (reputation), signer, and the parent process that dropped it. 2) Contain: If unsanctioned, isolate the host, kill the MeshAgent service/process, and block its outbound WSS destination at the proxy/firewall. 3) Hunt: Search other hosts for the same SHA256/service, look for co-located ransomware staging (rclone.exe, GPO logon scripts, .SINOBI files) and enumerate the account that installed the service.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where FileName has "meshagent"
    or ProcessVersionInfoOriginalFileName has "MeshAgent"
    or ProcessVersionInfoProductName has "MeshCentral"
| where not(FolderPath has_any (@"\Program Files\Mesh Agent\", @"\Program Files (x86)\Mesh Agent\"))
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, ProcessIntegrityLevel, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName has "meshagent"
| where NewProcessName !has @"\Program Files\Mesh Agent\"
| where SubjectUserName !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName, TokenElevationType
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: MeshAgent Execution From Non-Standard Path

Zoho Assist Unattended Agent deployment (Warlock / Storm-2603 ransomware) AIInstallation Medium
Hunts execution of Zoho Assist Unattended Agent binaries, the RMM tool Warlock (Storm-2603) operators install for persistent, session-independent remote control ahead of encryption. Flags the agent/installer binaries especially when run non-interactively or as SYSTEM. Rationale: Anchors on the corroborated report detail that Warlock/Storm-2603 deployed the Zoho Assist Unattended Agent for persistence; the unattended/SYSTEM context distinguishes attacker deployment from interactive helpdesk use. Cross-checked Talos IR Q2 2026 and Intel471 RMM-abuse writeup. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.talosintelligence.com/ir-trends-q2-2026/ • https://www.intel471.com/blog/understanding-and-threat-hunting-for-rmm-software-misuse
ATT&CKT1219 T1543.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Sanctioned Zoho Assist use by an internal or outsourced IT helpdesk
  • MSP performing legitimate unattended-access provisioning
  • Software inventory/patching workflows that bundle Zoho
  • User-initiated Zoho support session for a real ticket
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !in~ ("helpdesk-svc","msp-support") and DeviceName !in~ ("<known-helpdesk-hosts>")
Response runbook
1) Triage: Confirm whether Zoho Assist is an approved support tool for this host; check who initiated it, the parent process, and whether an unattended (session-independent) install was performed. 2) Contain: If unauthorized, isolate the host, remove the Zoho Assist Unattended service, and block Zoho Assist gateway domains for the affected segment. 3) Hunt: Enumerate other hosts with the same binary/service, review for follow-on ransomware TTPs (rclone staging, shadow-copy deletion, GPO logon scripts) and audit the service account used for install.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ProcessVersionInfoCompanyName has "ZOHO"
    or ProcessVersionInfoProductName has "Zoho Assist"
    or FileName in~ ("ZA_Access.exe","ZA_Connect.exe","ZMAgent.exe")
    or ProcessCommandLine has "Zoho_Assist"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("unattended","install","silent") or ProcessIntegrityLevel == "System"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, ProcessIntegrityLevel, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName has_any ("ZA_Access.exe","ZA_Connect.exe","ZMAgent.exe","Zoho_Assist")
| where SubjectUserName !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName, TokenElevationType
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Email-hiding inbox rules created post-compromise (BEC / mailbox concealment) AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts creation/modification of Exchange Online inbox rules that delete, mark-as-read, redirect, or move messages to hidden folders — the concealment step Talos IR observed after auth-abuse account takeover, often preceding large outbound email bursts. Distinct from generic phishing-click detections. Rationale: Grounds on the corroborated Talos IR finding of email-hiding rule creation (T1564.008) and outbound-email spikes after auth abuse; scoping to delete/redirect/mark-read parameters keeps only concealment-intent rules rather than benign filing rules. Cross-checked Talos IR Q2 2026. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.talosintelligence.com/ir-trends-q2-2026/
ATT&CKT1564.008 T1114.003
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • User legitimately auto-filing newsletters into folders or Deleted Items
  • Executive assistant configuring forwarding to a shared mailbox
  • Mailbox migration/cleanup tooling that rewrites rules in bulk
  • Out-of-office or VIP triage rules marking mail as read
Suppression filter
| where not (Parameters has "MoveToFolder" and Parameters !has_any ("DeleteMessage","ForwardTo","RedirectTo","Deleted Items"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: Review the rule parameters and the creating IP/UserAgent against the user's baseline; check if the same session had a risky/device-code sign-in or impossible travel. 2) Contain: If malicious, remove the inbox rule, revoke sessions, reset credentials + re-register MFA, and search sent items for fraudulent/BEC messages. 3) Hunt: Correlate with outbound email volume spikes (e.g., thousands of messages), other users with identical rule patterns, and OAuth app consents from the same source IP.
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where Application == "Microsoft Exchange Online"
| where ActionType in ("New-InboxRule","Set-InboxRule","UpdateInboxRules","Update-InboxRules")
| extend Raw = tostring(RawEventData)
| where Raw has_any ("DeleteMessage","Deleted Items","MarkAsRead","Junk Email","MoveToFolder","ForwardTo","RedirectTo")
| project Timestamp, AccountDisplayName, AccountObjectId, IPAddress, ActionType, ObjectName, Raw
| order by Timestamp desc
OfficeActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where Operation in ("New-InboxRule","Set-InboxRule","UpdateInboxRules")
| where Parameters has_any ("DeleteMessage","Deleted Items","MarkAsRead","Junk Email","MoveToFolder","ForwardTo","RedirectTo")
| project TimeGenerated, UserId, ClientIP, Operation, OfficeWorkload, Parameters
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.

Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;

| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"

   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
